questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of schizophrenia in people with intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Schizophrenia is approximately 3 times more common in those with intellectual disability than in the general population. Most studies report a prevalence of around 3% for schizophrenia.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 826.

questions.question_text: Angelman syndrome is characterised by
questions.explanation:
Angelman syndrome is characterised by severe/profound intellectual disability. Approximately 86% of individuals have epilepsy.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 808.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Fragile X syndrome is not correct?

options.text: It accounts for 10-12% of intellectual disability in males
It is associated with trinucleotide CGG repeats at a fragile site on the Y chromosome
It is associated with mitral valve prolapse
Brain imaging may show reduced posterior cerebellar vermis

correct_answer.text: It is associated with trinucleotide CGG repeats at a fragile site on the Y chromosome

correct_answers.text: It is associated with trinucleotide CGG repeats at a fragile site on the Y chromosome

questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is a common inherited cause of intellectual disability (ID) with X-linked dominant transmission. Penetrance is low, but greater in males than females due to the 'protective' effects of the second normal X chromosome in females. Fragile X syndrome accounts for 10-12% of ID in men. The syndrome is associated with a large sequence of triplet repeats (CGG) at a fragile site on the X chromosome (Xq27.3). The gene sequence is designated FMR-1. Clinical features include a large head, large ears, elongated face, high arched palate, short stature, mitral valve prolapse, poor muscle tone, large testes (macroorchidism), and hyperextensible joints. Brain imaging may show enlarged ventricles, enlarged hippocampus and caudate nuclei, and reduced posterior cerebellar vermis.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 814.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: Autism is most commonly associated with
questions.explanation:
80% of patients with autism have mild to moderate intellectual disability. The cause of autism is unknown, but a number of hypotheses exist: genetic (in Down syndrome and Fragile X); obstetric complications; toxic agents; pre/post-natal infections (with maternal rubella); autoimmune; and association with neurological disorders (e.g. tuberous sclerosis).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 822.

questions.question_text: Asperger syndrome is characterised by delays in
questions.explanation:
People with Asperger syndrome show no language delay and their cognitive development is not marked by an overall delay but by specific impairments in certain areas such as the executive functions. Children with autism spectrum disorder of an Asperger syndrome type often have difficulty deciphering the subtleties of non-verbal communication such as tone of voice, gestures, facial expressions, and body language.
Ref: Mirkovic B, Gérardin P. Asperger's syndrome: What to consider?. L'encephale. 2019 Apr 1;45(2):169-74.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is seen in hands of people with Down syndrome?

options.text: Short, broad hands with a single palmar crease

questions.explanation:
Clinical features in the hands of people with Down syndrome include short, broad hands with a single palmar crease, syndactyly (webbed fingers), clinodactyly (incurving of fingers), and altered dermatoglyphics.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 806.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old boy with severe intellectual disability has a round face with hypertelorism, slanting palpebral fissures, broad flat nose, and an infantile cat-like cry. Which of the following conditions is he most likely to suffer from?
questions.explanation:
Cri-du-chat syndrome is a partial monosomy; karyotype 5p- (varies from deletion of a small band at 5p15.2 to the entire arm of 5p). The infant has a characteristic high-pitched cry that resembles a cat. Clinical features include microcephaly, rounded face, hypertelorism, micrognathia, dental malocclusion, epicanthic folds, low-set ears, hypotonia, and severe/profound intellectual disability.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 808.

questions.question_text: In people with intellectual disability, which of the following is associated with an increased prevalence of depression?
questions.explanation:
Reported prevalence estimates of depression in people with intellectual disability (ID) vary greatly (from almost non-existent to 39%). Those living in an institution show a higher prevalence of depression than those living with their families. More depressive symptoms are associated with increased age. Depressive disorders are reported to occur more often in people with mild to moderate ID than in those with severe to profound ID. Note that co-occurring psychiatric disorders are common in people with ID. The pooled prevalence of any co-occurring psychiatric disorder in ID is approximately 34%.
Ref: Scheirs JG et al. The Prevalence and Diagnosis of Depression in People with Mild or Borderline Intellectual Disability: Multiple Instrument Testing Tells Us More. Journal of Mental Health Research in Intellectual Disabilities. 2022 Feb 12:1-3.
Mazza MG et al. Prevalence of co-occurring psychiatric disorders in adults and adolescents with intellectual disability: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities. 2020 Mar;33(2):126-38.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is classified in ICD-11 as a developmental learning disorder?
questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading (dyslexia) is characterised by significant and persistent difficulties in learning academic skills related to reading, such as word reading accuracy, reading fluency, and reading comprehension. In ICD-11, other developmental learning disorders can be diagnosed with impairment in written expression, with impairment in mathematics, and with other specified impairment of learning.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 678.

questions.question_text: Prior to the introduction of DSM-5, a multi-axial system was used by DSM-IV. DSM-IV coded mental retardation on which of the following axes?
questions.explanation:
DSM-IV was a multi-axial diagnostic system, using five axes. Axis 2 coded any personality disorder and any mental handicap. This multi-axial approach was abandoned in DSM-5.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 11.

questions.question_text: As defined by the UK's Royal College of Psychiatrists, which of the following is not a criterion of 'challenging behaviour' in those with intellectual disabilities? It threatens the

options.text: Quality of life of the individual

questions.explanation:
The UK's Royal College of Psychiatrists defines challenging behaviour as 'behaviour of such an intensity, frequency, or duration as to threaten the quality of life and/or physical safety of the individual or others and is likely to lead to responses that are restrictive, aversive, or result in exclusion'.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 828.

questions.question_text: What level of intellectual disability is most associated with offending behaviour?

options.text: Intellectual disability is not associated with offending behaviour

questions.explanation:
The rate of offending in people with intellectual disability is consistently higher than that of the general population. Offending occurs more often in people with milder forms of intellectual disability than in those with severe intellectual disability. Profound and severe intellectual disability may be associated with disturbed/challenging behaviour but would rarely come to the attention of the criminal justice system.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 747, 832.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old man with severe intellectual disability presents to the outpatient clinic with his live-in caregiver who reports that the patient intermittently engages in self-injurious behaviour. The caregiver remembers hearing several years ago that naltrexone might be helpful in such situations. Current evidence for the use of naltrexone in the management of self-injurious behaviour suggests which of the following?

options.text: There is minimal and conflicting evidence for the efficacy of naltrexone
Naltrexone is the gold-standard treatment for self-injurious behaviour
RCTs have consistently shown benefit for naltrexone over placebo
The clinical use of naltrexone for self-injurious behaviours is increasing
The caregiver is mistaken; naltrexone has never been used for this purpose

correct_answer.text: There is minimal and conflicting evidence for the efficacy of naltrexone

correct_answers.text: There is minimal and conflicting evidence for the efficacy of naltrexone

questions.explanation:
Naltrexone is a pure opioid antagonist that exhibits high affinity for mu-opioid binding sites. Its role in the treatment of self-injurious behaviours (SIBs) evolved from the theory that SIBs stimulate release of endogenous endorphins, which may drive some of the observed repetitive behavioural patterns. Naltrexone was of great interest in the late 1980s and early 1990s. However, available literature has demonstrated conflicting efficacy results and is limited to case reports, small case series, and small controlled studies. The evidence regarding the use of naltrexone for treatment of SIBs is minimal and conflicting at best, and clinical use has largely fallen out of favour. At present, naltrexone should be reserved for those patients who are refractory to other treatment options.
Ref: Sabus A et al. Management of Self-injurious Behaviors in Children with Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Pharmacotherapy Overview. Pharmacotherapy: The Journal of Human Pharmacology and Drug Therapy. 2019 Jun;39(6):645-64.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with Down syndrome is seen in the intellectual disability clinic. He may be developing Alzheimer disease. Which of the following tests would be most useful in establishing a diagnosis?

options.text: Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities
Cambridge Examination for Mental Disorders of the Elderly

correct_answer.text: Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities

correct_answers.text: Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities

questions.explanation:
Formerly known as the Dementia Questionnaire for Mentally Retarded Persons (DMR), The Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities (DLD) is used to facilitate the diagnosis of dementia in persons with intellectual disability, based on observations of caregivers.
Ref: Evenhuis HM. The dementia questionnaire for people with learning disabilities. In Neuropsychological assessments of dementia in down syndrome and intellectual disabilities 2018. pp. 43-56.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is licensed for the treatment of self-injurious behaviour and aggression in patients with intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Lithium is licensed for the treatment of self-injurious behaviour and aggression in individuals with intellectual disability (ID). Lithium is perhaps best considered when there is a sub-syndromal or nonspecific 'affective component'. Some authorities suggest that challenging behaviour may occur in the context of very rapid cycling bipolar disorder in some individuals with severe and profound ID.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 800.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning Fragile X syndrome (FXS) and intellectual disability/IQ?

options.text: In the FMR1 gene, CGG repeats in the range of 5-44 are considered 'pre-mutation'
Individuals with a higher number of CGG repeats have lower IQ
Females with FXS show more severe intellectual disability than males with FXS
Those with mosaicism have more severe intellectual disability than those without
Higher levels of FMRP are found in those with the lowest IQ

correct_answer.text: Individuals with a higher number of CGG repeats have lower IQ

correct_answers.text: Individuals with a higher number of CGG repeats have lower IQ

questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome (FXS) occurs as a result of FMR1 gene hypermethylation due to an unstable CGG triplet repeat expansion (>200 repeats) in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene located on the X chromosome, which leads to gene methylation, inactivation, and resultant loss of fragile X mental retardation protein expression (FMRP). The normal number of repeats within the FMR1 gene ranges from 5-44; a repeat number of 45-54 is considered a grey zone. A repeat number of 55-200 is called a pre-mutation and is associated with pathological conditions that differ from FXS. Because FXS is an X-linked genetic disorder, females with FXS are typically less severely affected than males with FXS due to the variability of X-chromosome inactivation in females. IQ directly correlates with the levels of FMRP production: higher levels of FMRP (and lower CGG repeats) are found in individuals with an IQ above 70. Those individuals with 'size-mosaicism' (full mutation plus premutation, grey zone, or normal alleles) have higher IQs than those without mosaicism. A drop in IQ is noted especially in pre-adolescent (8-12 years) boys with FXS that stabilises by puberty (age 15). No further drop occurs after this, and, in fact, the adaptive skills improve continuously in most males. Hence, FXS cannot be classed as a degenerative disease.
Ref: Razak KA et al. Developmental studies in fragile X syndrome. Journal of neurodevelopmental disorders. 2020 Dec;12(1):1-5.
Ciaccio C et al. Fragile X syndrome: a review of clinical and molecular diagnoses. Italian journal of pediatrics. 2017 Dec;43(1):1-2.
Schmitt LM, Shaffer RC, Hessl D, Erickson C. Executive function in fragile X syndrome: a systematic review. Brain Sciences. 2019 Jan 16;9(1):15.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of Cornelia de Lange syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a rare genetic disorder associated with a lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein (PAPPA) linked to chromosome 9q33. As a similar phenotype is associated with trisomy 5p, ring chromosome 3. Individuals with Cornelia de Lange syndrome have severe to profound intellectual disability. Clinical features include short stature, hypertrichosis (hirsutism, synophrys (continuous eyebrows), long eyelashes), prominent philtrum, small upturned nose, thin down-turning upper lip, microcephaly, low-set ears, and small hands and feet. It is also associated with GI problems (in particular reflux), congenital heart defects, visual and hearing problems, skin problems, epilepsy, and death in infancy. Behavioural problems include self-injury, temper tantrums, stereotypic movements, and twirling.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 819.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is most commonly associated with anxiety?
questions.explanation:
Williams Syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from a microdeletion of 7q11.23, is characterized by unique craniofacial features and cardiovascular abnormalities. Individuals generally have mild to moderate intellectual disability but good expressive language development. Williams syndrome is associated with anxiety and fears. In some cross-sectional studies, >70% of individuals were above the cut-off for anxiety disorders. Often there is abnormal attachment behaviour manifested as anxiety, poor peer relationships, and hypersensitivity (or conversely as social disinhibition and excessive friendliness).
Ref: Shaffer, R.C., et al., 2022. Systematic Review: Emotion Dysregulation in Syndromic Causes of Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities. Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaac.2022.06.020

questions.question_text: Self-talk seems to be particularly common in children with
questions.explanation:
The behavioural phenotype of Down syndrome includes being passive, affable, demonstrating hyperactivity in childhood, being stubborn, and often talking or mumbling to themselves (private speech).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.
Dykens EM et al. Psychiatric disorders in adolescents and young adults with Down syndrome and other intellectual disabilities. Journal of neurodevelopmental disorders. 2015 Dec;7(1):1-8.

questions.question_text: What percentage of persons with intellectual disabilies have severe intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Mild intellectual disability (ID) represents approximately 85% of persons with intellectual disabilities; moderate ID 10%; severe ID 4%; and profound ID 1-2%.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 95.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of epilepsy in people with mild intellectual disability is about
questions.explanation:
Epilepsy is more common in people with intellectual disability (ID) than in the general population. The prevalence of epilepsy varies with the severity and cause of ID. It is higher in severe ID (30-50%) than in mild ID (15-20%). Epilepsy is common in people with ID of various causes, such as Down syndrome 5-10%; Fragile X syndrome 25%; Angelman syndrome 90%; and Rett syndrome 90%.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 824.
Sun JJ, et al. Epilepsy related multimorbidity, polypharmacy and risks in adults with intellectual disabilities: a national study. Journal of Neurology. 2022 May;269(5):2750-60.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is NOT suggestive of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?

options.text: Diffuse interictal slow spike-waves on waking EEG
Most often appears between ages of 3 and 5

questions.explanation:
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is a severe form of epilepsy with onset in childhood (age of onset usually before 8 years; peak between 3 and 5 years). The syndrome is defined by a triad of multiple drug-resistant seizure types (tonic, atonic, and atypical absences); a specific EEG pattern showing bursts of slow spike-wave complexes or generalised paroxysmal fast activity; and intellectual disability. The interictal EEG pattern of slow spike-waves is associated with LGS, though not pathognomonic of the disorder. Atonic seizures are common in LGS; they are also known as 'drop attacks' or 'drop seizures' because they are characterised by a sudden loss of muscle tone that can result in the patient falling to the ground. LGS has deleterious effects on intellectual functioning. Cognitive impairment usually becomes more apparent over time, and within 5 years of onset, serious intellectual problems have developed in most patients.
Ref: Asadi-Pooya AA. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: a comprehensive review. Neurological Sciences. 2018 Mar 1;39(3):403-14.
Strzelczyk A, Schubert-Bast S. Expanding the treatment landscape for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: current and future strategies. CNS drugs. 2021 Jan;35(1):61-83.

questions.question_text: A male patient has autistic traits, conversational rigidity, palilalia, anxiety, and poor eye contact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the most common single gene cause of autism. Behavioural features of fragile X syndrome appear to be similar to those seen in ADHD and autism, including hand flapping/waving, repetitive mannerisms, shyness, gaze avoidance, poor peer relationships, communication difficulties (e.g. delayed language development, conversational rigidity, perseveration, echolalia, palilalia, cluttering, and over-detailed/circumstantial speech), and psychiatric problems (e.g. prominent depression/anxiety).
Ref: Razak KA et al. Developmental studies in fragile X syndrome. Journal of neurodevelopmental disorders. 2020 Dec;12(1):1-5.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 814.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sleep patterns is commonly seen in Rett syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Sleep disturbances are relatively common in Rett syndrome. Typically, patients suffer from initial and/or intermediate insomnia (i.e., difficulty falling asleep and frequent awakenings during the night). Complaints of excessive somnolence, and of initiating and maintaining sleep are most prevalent in Rett syndrome.
Ref: Persico AM et al. The psychopharmacology of autism spectrum disorder and Rett syndrome. In Handbook of clinical neurology 2019 Jan 1 (Vol. 165, pp. 391-414). Elsevier.
Spruyt K. Sleep problems in individuals with Rett Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sleep Epidemiology. 2022 Apr 14:1-12.

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a 'subcultural' rather than a biological cause for intellectual disability?

options.text: Equal distribution across families of different types of socio-economic status
Intellectual ability is impaired in family members
Males are more commonly affected than females

correct_answer.text: Intellectual ability is impaired in family members

correct_answers.text: Intellectual ability is impaired in family members

questions.explanation:
Although the concept of 'psychosocial' causation (due to physical and emotional neglect) for intellectual disability is controversial, mild or borderline intellectual impairment is more common in families of lower socio-economic status (SES). This is best viewed as a cultural norm, and individuals generally have no, or only minor, impairments in adaptive functioning. Generally, the intellectual ability of family members is also in the borderline range, dysmorphic characteristics are less likely, and other impairments or disabilities are unusual ('subcultural' intellectual disability). This is in contrast to biological causation where impairments are more significant, there is no difference in SES, parents and siblings are usually of normal intelligence, and dysmorphic features are more common.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 791.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common aetiological factor in developing intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Aetiological contributions to intellectual disability may be classified based on the timing of the causative event: 50-70% of cases attributable to a prenatal factor (during embryogenesis), 10-20% to a perinatal factor (around the time of delivery), and 5-10% to a postnatal factor (in the first years of life).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 794-795.

questions.question_text: Among people with intellectual disability, pica is more commonly seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Pica is characterised by persistent (>1 month) eating of non-nutritive substances at a developmentally inappropriate age (>1 year). It typically occurs during the 2 and 3 years of life, though may occur in young pregnant women. Common substances include dirt, stones, plastic, paper, hair, faeces, wood, string, etc. Pica is more frequent in people with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 694.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 162-163.

questions.question_text: Which of the following techniques is used to treat stuttering?
questions.explanation:
Treatment of stuttering falls into two general categories: indirect and direct. Indirect treatment does not use overt or explicit methods with the child. Rather, it targets parent counselling, and/or the use of the parent/clinician to model fluency facilitators for the child. Direct treatments usually explicitly teach the child to change something about the way the child speaks. Direct treatments may focus on obtaining 'smooth speech' through fluency shaping strategies based on prolonged speech principles that include gradual phonatory initiation, smooth transitions between words using imagery that appeals to children, or stuttering modification. The clinician and/or parent models a slow, relaxed speaking pattern that emphasises reduced rate, smooth articulatory transitions, and slightly prolonged consonants and vowels, while preserving the natural intonation and stress patterns.
Shenker RC, Santayana G. What are the options for the treatment of stuttering in preschool children? In Seminars in speech and language 2018 Sep (Vol. 39, No. 04). pp. 313-323.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is associated with skin picking?
questions.explanation:
The behavioural phenotype of Prader-Willi syndrome includes compulsive behaviour, hyperphagia, hoarding, impulsivity, emotional lability, tantrums, excessive daytime sleepiness, skin-picking, and aggression.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman who is pregnant for the first time is concerned about having a child with Down syndrome. What is the approximate incidence of Down syndrome per 1000 live births for women in her age group?
questions.explanation:
The incidence of Down syndrome per 1000 live births is approximately 0.5 for a woman under 25; 0.7 under the age of 30; 5 under 35; 25 under 40; and 34.6 over the age of 45. Most children with Down syndrome are born to mothers under the age of 35, due to the higher number of pregnancies in younger women.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: A mother who has a child with autism is expecting a second baby. What is the risk of autism in her second child?
questions.explanation:
Autism recurrence rates in large-scale population-based twin and family studies are 0.8 for identical twins, 0.2 for non-identical siblings, and 0.04 for second-degree relatives.
Ref: Bai D et al. Inherited risk for autism through maternal and paternal lineage. Biological psychiatry. 2020 Sep 15;88(6):480-7.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a sex chromosome monosomy?
questions.explanation:
Turner syndrome is a sex chromosome monosomy with karyotype 45,XO and female phenotype.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 817.

questions.question_text: Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely to cause intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Down syndrome is a trisomy of chromosome 21 and the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability (ID). IQ most often below 50 (range: low to high/moderate ID).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 806.

questions.question_text: The behavioural phenotype of Prader-Willi syndrome commonly includes which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The behavioural phenotype of Prader-Willi syndrome includes compulsive behaviour, hyperphagia, hoarding, impulsivity, emotional lability, tantrums, excessive daytime sleepiness, skin-picking, and aggression.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a postnatal factor that increases the risk of intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Postnatal factors (occurring in the first years of life) associated with intellectual disability include CNS infections, intracranial tumours, hypoxic brain injury, head injury (e.g. RTAs, household accidents, child abuse), exposure to toxic agents, and the psychosocial environment (i.e. deprivation).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 795.

questions.question_text: Those with Down syndrome who survive into their 40s and 50s show pathological brain changes similar to
questions.explanation:
Neuropathological changes similar to Alzheimer dementia are seen in individuals with Down syndrome over the age of 40. Other CNS abnormalities in Down syndrome include reduced brain weight, reduced gyri, cortical thinning, underdeveloped middle lobe of the cerebellum, reduced neuronal numbers in the cerebellum/locus caeruleus/basal forebrain, reduced cholinergic neurons, and epilepsy.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 807.

questions.question_text: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is characterised by
questions.explanation:
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an extremely rare recessive condition associated with a defect on the short arm of the X chromosome. A deficiency of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyl transferase leads to build up of uric acid. Severe compulsive self-mutilation is often seen, including biting of the lips, inside of the mouth, and fingers.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 816.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions is microcephaly a characteristic feature?
questions.explanation:
Clinical features of foetal alcohol syndrome include microcephaly, short palpebral fissures, small maxillae and mandibles, flat philtrum, thin upper lip, and short stature. The behavioural phenotype includes mild to moderate intellectual disability, irritability, inattention, and memory impairment.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 818.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 87.

questions.question_text: The most common inherited cause of intellectual disability is
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the most common single gene cause of autism. The syndrome affects around 1/4000 males and 1/8000 females.
Ref: Razak KA et al. Developmental studies in fragile X syndrome. Journal of neurodevelopmental disorders. 2020 Dec;12(1):1-5.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 814.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sex/gender-related differences is seen in autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?

options.text: Females are more likely than males to be diagnosed with ASD
During middle-childhood, girls are more likely to act out with reactive aggression
During middle-childhood, boys tend to withdraw socially
Females tend to demonstrate fewer restrictive, repetitive interests and behaviours
Males with less severe presentations often go undetected as compared to females

correct_answer.text: Females tend to demonstrate fewer restrictive, repetitive interests and behaviours

correct_answers.text: Females tend to demonstrate fewer restrictive, repetitive interests and behaviours

questions.explanation:
Males are four times more likely than females to be diagnosed with ASD. Less severe presentations in females are more likely to go undetected as compared to males. Females tend to demonstrate fewer restricted, repetitive interests and behaviours than males. During middle-childhood, gender differences in presentation differentially affect functioning. Boys may act out with reactive aggression or other behavioural symptoms when challenged or frustrated. Girls tend to withdraw socially and react with emotional changes to their social adjustment difficulties.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about velo-cardio-facial syndrome?

options.text: Large ears and wide palpebral fissures are common features
It is usually associated with severe intellectual disability
It occurs in around 1 in 2000 people
It is due to a chromosome 21 microdeletion
It is usually associated with dementia

correct_answer.text: It occurs in around 1 in 2000 people

correct_answers.text: It occurs in around 1 in 2000 people

questions.explanation:
Velo-cardio-facial (di George) syndrome is caused by a microdeletion of chromosome 22 (22q11.2). The incidence is 1:2000. Clinical features include intellectual disability (mild: two-thirds; moderate: one-third), cardiac abnormalities (75%), facial features (microcephaly, cleft palate, small mouth, long face, narrow palpebral fissure, minor ear abnormalities), hypocalcemia (60%), hypospadias, and long & thin hands. Associated behavioural and psychiatric disorders include schizophrenia and blunted/inappropriate affect.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 808.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with hypertrichosis and severe intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a rare genetic disorder associated with a lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein (PAPPA) linked to chromosome 9q33. A similar phenotype is associated with trisomy 5p, ring chromosome 3. Individuals with Cornelia de Lange syndrome have severe to profound intellectual disability. Clinical features include short stature, hypertrichosis (hirsutism, synophrys (continuous eyebrows), long eyelashes), prominent philtrum, small upturned nose, thin down-turning upper lip, microcephaly, low-set ears, and small hands and feet. It is also associated with GI problems (in particular reflux), congenital heart defects, visual and hearing problems, skin problems, epilepsy, and death in infancy. Behavioural problems include self-injury, temper tantrums, stereotypic movements, and twirling.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 819.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner?
questions.explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominant syndrome. The incidence is equal between males and females. Individuals show varying degrees (usually severe) of intellectual disability (50%).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 810.

questions.question_text: Prominent anxiety is most common in which of the following syndromes associated with intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the most common single gene cause of autism. Behavioural features of fragile X syndrome appear to be similar to those seen in ADHD and autism, including hand flapping/waving, repetitive mannerisms, shyness, gaze avoidance, poor peer relationships, communication difficulties (e.g. delayed language development, conversational rigidity, perseveration, echolalia, palilalia, cluttering, and over-detailed/circumstantial speech), and psychiatric problems (e.g. prominent depression/anxiety).
Ref: Razak KA et al. Developmental studies in fragile X syndrome. Journal of neurodevelopmental disorders. 2020 Dec;12(1):1-5.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 814.

questions.question_text: Happy disposition and paroxysmal laughter are features commonly seen in
questions.explanation:
Angelman ('happy puppet') syndrome is characterised by severe/profound intellectual disability. Approximately 86% of individuals have epilepsy. Other clinical features include happy disposition, paroxysmal laughter, absence of speech, hand flapping, clapping, ataxia (jerky limb movements, gait problems), and anecdotal love of water and music.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 808.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: A microdeletion on the paternal 15q12 chromosomal segment causes
questions.explanation:
Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disorder associated with a microdeletion on chromosome 15 (q11-13), usually on the paternal chromosome. 90% of cases are sporadic. The candidate gene is small nuclear ribonucleoprotein polypeptide (SNRPN). Males are more commonly affected (M:F = 4:3) and the incidence is 1:10,000-40,000.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 808.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: Predisposing factors for behavioural problems in children with intellectual disability include
questions.explanation:
Factors associated with behavioural disorders and challenging behaviour in intellectual disability include severe intellectual impairment, poor/absent language ability, poor social comprehension, high emotionality, hyperactivity, poor sociability, physical problems (e.g. epilepsy, cerebral palsy, cardiac problems, GI problems), visual/hearing impairment, and communication difficulties.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 828-829.

questions.question_text: Approximately 20% of those with autism spectrum disorders also have
questions.explanation:
Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) increase the risk of obesity. The prevalence of obesity in ASD is approximately 20-22%.
Ref: Kahathuduwa CN et al. The risk of overweight and obesity in children with autism spectrum disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Obesity Reviews. 2019 Dec;20(12):1667-79.

questions.question_text: Klinefelter syndrome is characterised by all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Klinefelter syndrome (karyotype 47,XXY) is one of the most common chromosomal disorders. It is seen in 1:1000 live male births. Clinical features include a variable degree of development of secondary sexual characteristics (with sparse body hair, hypogonadism, and gynaecomastia), taller than average stature (by around 4cms), thin build, and median IQ of approximately 90 with skewed distribution (most in 60-70 range). There is an uncertain association with psychiatric disorders.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 817.

questions.question_text: What is the mode of inheritance of Fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is a common inherited cause of intellectual disability (ID) with X-linked dominant transmission. Penetrance is low, but greater in males than females due to the 'protective' effects of the second normal X chromosome in females. Fragile X syndrome accounts for 10-12% of ID in men.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 814.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about the epidemiology of autism?

options.text: It is more common in children who have had the MMR vaccine
It is more common in girls than boys
It is more common in parents of higher socio-economic status
Monozygotic twin concordance is greater than 90%

questions.explanation: Explanation:Twin and family studies consistently demonstrate that autism has a particularly large genetic contribution, with a heritability of approximately 80-90%. Autism is highly heritable and is among the most heritable common medical conditions.Ref: Lord C et al. Autism spectrum disorder. Nature reviews Disease primers. 2020 Jan 16;6(1):1-23.Sandin S et al. The heritability of autism spectrum disorder. Jama. 2017 Sep 26;318(12):1182-4.

questions.question_text: In individuals with intellectual disability, self-injurious behaviour occurs most frequently between the ages of
questions.explanation: Explanation:Many individuals with intellectual disability suffer from self-injurious behaviour, which includes head-banging, head hitting, and other behaviours that can cause physical trauma. Self-injurious behaviour in those with intellectual disability often emerges between 2-3 years of age. It is more frequent and severe in childhood and adolescence. The severity can decrease over the course of adulthood.Ref: Hagopian LP, Leoni M. Self-injurious behavior among individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders: Acta Psychopathol. 2017;3(5):70.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common chromosomal aberration seen in Down syndrome?

options.text: Mosaicism with both normal and trisomic cell lines
Mosaicism with only trisomic cells present

questions.explanation: Explanation:Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability. Full trisomy 21 (nondisjunction) occurs in around 95% of cases. Extra chromosome 21 material can also occur due to Robertsonian translocation in 5% cases (long arm of chromosome 21 is attached to another chromosome, usually chromosome 14; also 13, 15, and 22 described). In 2-5% cases, there is a mixture of normal and trisomic cell lines, known as mosaic Down syndrome.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 806.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an X-linked recessive condition?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Hunter syndrome is an X-linked recessive syndrome caused by a deficiency of iduronate sulfatase (mapped to Xq27-28) and consequent accumulation of glycosaminoglycans. The incidence is 1:100,000.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 816.

questions.question_text: In people with intellectual disability, which of the following is NOT a common symptom of PTSD?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Symptoms of irritability or outbursts of anger, which can manifest as physical aggression, are common symptoms in those with intellectual disability suffering from PTSD. Aggressive behaviours can be symptoms of trauma. Those who experience traumatic life events, in both childhood and adulthood, have a significantly higher risk of aggression, self-injurious behaviour, and symptoms of psychological distress.Ref: McNally P et al. Trauma experiences of people with an intellectual disability and their implications: A scoping review. Journal of applied research in intellectual disabilities. 2021 Jul;34(4):927-49.

questions.question_text: In people with intellectual disability (ID) and PTSD, which of the following is true?

options.text: Lack of verbal abilities may limit reporting of symptoms
Trauma is usually disclosed very soon after its occurrence
People with ID rarely experience trauma
Symptoms of PTSD resolve rapidly in those with ID

correct_answer.text: Lack of verbal abilities may limit reporting of symptoms

correct_answers.text: Lack of verbal abilities may limit reporting of symptoms

questions.explanation: Explanation:People with an intellectual disability (ID) are significantly more likely to experience adverse life events, abuse, and trauma than the general population. However, assessment for PTSD is challenging because individuals with ID have difficulties in self-report. Often abuse is only revealed or discovered years after its occurrence, even in cases involving good verbal abilities. Re-experiencing involving classic flashbacks is only rarely described in individuals with good verbal abilities. It is unlikely that symptoms of re-experiencing are dependent on a certain level of cognitive or verbal ability, so the sparseness of reports of re-experiencing are more likely explained by a combination of the intrapsychic nature of these symptoms and patients' lack of verbal abilities. Abuse and other adverse events can lead to long-lasting psychological damage, affecting the lives of individuals with ID and their families for years.Ref: McNally P et al. Trauma experiences of people with an intellectual disability and their implications: A scoping review. Journal of applied research in intellectual disabilities. 2021 Jul;34(4):927-49.Kildahl AN et al. Identification of post-traumatic stress disorder in individuals with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability: A systematic review. Journal of Mental Health Research in Intellectual Disabilities. 2019 Apr 3;12(1-2):1-25.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man with cerebral palsy and chronic epilepsy resides in a care home. His communication skills are very limited. He has limited ability to self-care, cannot contribute to self-maintenance despite complete supervision, and requires 24-hour supervised care. The severity of his intellectual disability is best classified as
questions.explanation: Ref: Williams F et al. Alcohol use disorders in people with intellectual disability. BJPsych Advances. 2018 Jul;24(4):264-72.

questions.question_text: The IQ of an 11-year-old boy is evaluated as 75. Which of the following is true?

options.text: Low IQ at age 11 is a definite predictor of conduct disorder at a later age
There will be a further drop in IQ after adolescence
There is an increased risk of schizophrenia compared to general population
He falls two percentiles below the average IQ of the standard population

correct_answer.text: There is an increased risk of schizophrenia compared to general population

correct_answers.text: There is an increased risk of schizophrenia compared to general population

questions.explanation: Explanation:Individuals with borderline intellectual function have an IQ of 71-84 (1-2 standard deviations below the mean on a normal curve). They are twice as likely to develop a psychiatric disorder, including schizophrenia, as people with average or above average IQ.Ref: Hassiotis A et al. Association of Borderline Intellectual Functioning and Adverse Childhood Experience with adult psychiatric morbidity. Findings from a British birth cohort. BMC psychiatry. 2019 Dec;19(1):1-9.

questions.question_text: Of the following, the risk of developing Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome is most increased by

options.text: A family history of Alzheimer disease
Mild intellectual disability rather than severe intellectual disability

correct_answer.text: A family history of Alzheimer disease

correct_answers.text: A family history of Alzheimer disease

questions.explanation: Explanation:Almost all adults with Down syndrome (DS) develop Alzheimer disease (AD)-like neuropathology by 40 years of age. AD is characterised by a long asymptomatic preclinical stage in which amyloid pathology develops approximately 15-20 years before any cognitive impairment is observed. This preclinical stage is present in the autosomal dominant forms of AD and in early-onset AD associated with DS. The evidence is compelling that an increased dosage of APP (an HSA1 gene that encodes amyloid precursor protein) in trisomy 21 is necessary for an increased risk of AD in people with DS. The cognitive decline needs to be understood in the context of the existing cognitive phenotype and individual risk, including the APOE genotype, as the presence of the APOE E4 allele seems to increase risk of earlier cognitive decline due to AD.Ref: Antonarakis SE et al. Down syndrome. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2020 Jan;6(1):9.

questions.question_text: The highest incidence of intellectual disabilities is seen in
questions.explanation: Explanation:The prevalence of intellectual disability (ID) at any one time is estimated to range from 1-3% of the population. The incidence of ID is difficult to calculate because mild disabilities may be unrecognised until middle childhood. The highest incidence of ID is reported in school-age children, with a peak at ages 10-14 years. ID is about 1.5 times more common among males than females.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 100.

questions.question_text: Clinical features of Prader-Willi syndrome include all except
questions.explanation: Explanation:Clinical features of Prader-Willi syndrome include hypotonia, failure to thrive in infancy, obesity, small hands and feet, micro-orchidism, cryptorchidism, short stature, almond-shaped eyes, fair hair and light skin, flat face, scoliosis, orthopaedic problems, mild to moderate intellectual disability, and hyperphagia.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 808.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true of offending in the intellectual disability (ID) population?

options.text: Moderate ID is strongly associated with homicide
Conviction for arson leads to a fixed prison sentence
Most offences are committed by those with borderline and mild ID
People with ID commit the majority of violent offences
Fire setting is the most commonly committed offence

correct_answer.text: Most offences are committed by those with borderline and mild ID

correct_answers.text: Most offences are committed by those with borderline and mild ID

questions.explanation: Explanation:Offending occurs more often in people with milder form of intellectual disability (ID) than in those with severe ID. People with ID are at increased risk for crimes of aggression, sexual offending, and arson.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 747, 832.

questions.question_text: Epilepsy is present in nearly 90 percent of individuals with
questions.explanation: Explanation:Epilepsy is more common in people with intellectual disability (ID) than in the general population. The prevalence of epilepsy varies with the severity and cause of ID. It is higher in severe ID (30-50%) than in mild ID (15-20%). Epilepsy is common in people with ID of various causes, such as Down syndrome 5-10%; Fragile X syndrome 25%; Angelman syndrome 90%; and Rett syndrome 90%.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 824.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with tall stature?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Klinefelter syndrome (karyotype 47,XXY) is one of the most common chromosomal disorders. It is seen in 1:1000 live male births. Clinical features include a variable degree of development of secondary sexual characteristics (with sparse body hair, hypogonadism, and gynaecomastia), taller than average stature (by around 4cms), thin build, and median IQ of approximately 90 with skewed distribution (most in 60-70 range).Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 817.

questions.question_text: A 'subcultural' rather than a biological explanation for intellectual disability is supported by which of the following observations?

options.text: Normal distribution of intellectual disability across socio-economic groups
Borderline IQ in parents and siblings
Presence of moderate or severe intellectual disability

correct_answer.text: Borderline IQ in parents and siblings

correct_answers.text: Borderline IQ in parents and siblings

questions.explanation: Explanation:Although the concept of 'psychosocial' causation (due to physical and emotional neglect) for intellectual disability is controversial, mild or borderline intellectual impairment is more common in families of lower socio-economic status (SES). This is best viewed as a cultural norm, and individuals generally have no, or only minor, impairments in adaptive functioning. Generally, the intellectual ability of family members is also in the borderline range, dysmorphic characteristics are less likely, and other impairments or disabilities are unusual ('subcultural' intellectual disability). This is in contrast to biological causation where impairments are more significant, there is no difference in SES, parents and siblings are usually of normal intelligence, and dysmorphic features are more common.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 791.

questions.question_text: In adults with intellectual disability, dysphagia is a known side effect of which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Medications that depress the central nervous system, including clonazepam and other benzodiazepines, can lead to a decrease in awareness and voluntary muscle control which may affect swallowing in people with intellectual disability.Ref: Morton-Nance S. Drug-induced dysphagia and the high-risk effect on people with intellectual disabilities. Learning Disability Practice. 2020 Nov 26;23(6).

questions.question_text: The most common cause of death in Down syndrome is
questions.explanation: Explanation:Cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases account for 75% of mortality in Down syndrome. The leading causes of death are pneumonia and other infectious lung disease.Ref: Colvin KL, Yeager ME. What people with Down Syndrome can teach us about cardiopulmonary disease. European Respiratory Review. 2017 Mar 31;26(143).

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is seen almost exclusively in girls?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Rett syndrome is believed to be caused by a dominant X-linked gene. It is a degenerative disorder that almost exclusively affects females.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 103.Persico AM et al. The psychopharmacology of autism spectrum disorder and Rett syndrome. In Handbook of clinical neurology 2019 Jan 1 (Vol. 165, pp. 391-414). Elsevier.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders associated with intellectual disability is not a genetic deletion or duplication syndrome?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Klinefelter syndrome (karyotype 47,XXY) is one of the most common chromosomal disorders. It is a sex chromosome trisomy.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 817.

questions.question_text: Hypercalcemia with supravalvular aortic stenosis and elfin facial features are characteristic of
questions.explanation: Explanation:Clinical features of Williams syndrome include hypercalcemia (in 50%) with supravalvular aortic stenosis and elfin facial features. The syndrome is associated with anxiety and fears. Often there is abnormal attachment behaviour manifested as anxiety, poor peer relationships, and hypersensitivity (or conversely as social disinhibition and excessive friendliness). Verbal skills are often better than motor and visuospatial skills.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 809.

questions.question_text: The presence of extraordinary proficiency in one isolated skill, despite intellectual disability in other domains, is called
questions.explanation: Explanation:Of individuals with autism, a minority ('savants') may have 'islands of precocity' against a background of intellectual disability (i.e. isolated abilities, e.g. incredible memory or arithmetic skills).Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 823.

questions.question_text: A young boy displayed delayed developmental milestones. He learned to do basic self-care but struggled significantly at school, eventually dropping out. Upon reaching adulthood, he was able to live on his own, but his family came by regularly to bring food and assist with transportation and appointments. What is his level of intellectual disability?
questions.explanation: Ref: Williams F et al. Alcohol use disorders in people with intellectual disability. BJPsych Advances. 2018 Jul;24(4):264-72.

questions.question_text: Two siblings both have Fragile X syndrome. One child has severe intellectual disability (ID) and multiple physical and behavioural features of Fragile X. The other child has mild ID and very subtle clinical features. What is the most likely explanation for these differences?

options.text: One child is significantly older than the other
The child with mild ID has been misdiagnosed
One child is male and the other is female
The child with severe ID has experienced abuse

correct_answer.text: One child is male and the other is female

correct_answers.text: One child is male and the other is female

questions.explanation: Explanation:Fragile X syndrome (FXS) results from >200 CGG trinucleotide repeat expansions in the 5" untranslated region of the Fragile X Mental Retardation 1 Gene (FMR1). The resulting hyper-methylation and silencing of FMR protein (FMRP) production disrupts synaptic structure and function, leading to neural hyper-excitability and atypical brain development. Because FXS is an X-linked genetic disorder, females with FXS are typically less severely affected than males with FXS due to the variability of X-chromosome inactivation in females. Females with FXS who demonstrate a greater degree of methylation and lower FMRP levels have a phenotype more similar to males with FXS, whereas females with less methylation and greater FMRP levels demonstrate more subtle clinical features.Ref: Schmitt LM et al. Executive function in fragile X syndrome: a systematic review. Brain Sciences. 2019 Jan 16;9(1):15.

questions.question_text: The Special Education Needs & Disability Act of 2001 (UK) requires schools to draw up accessibility strategies for children with intellectual disabilities. The aim of this programme is to facilitate

options.text: the inclusion of some pupils without intellectual disabilities in special needs schools
the early provision of special needs education to pupils with intellectual disabilities
the inclusion of pupils with intellectual disabilities in mainstream schools
the enrolment of pupils with intellectual disabilities in special schools
the identification of gifted pupils in mainstream schools and provide them with special education

correct_answer.text: the inclusion of pupils with intellectual disabilities in mainstream schools

correct_answers.text: the inclusion of pupils with intellectual disabilities in mainstream schools

questions.explanation: Explanation:SENDA provisions increase access to a place in a mainstream school for children with special educational needs.Ref: https://adc.bmj.com/content/86/6/427

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about schizophrenia in individuals with intellectual disability is incorrect?

options.text: Patients are less likely to have complex delusional ideas
The rate is raised threefold over the general population
Thought disorder is probably more evident
Age of onset tends to be earlier
It is nearly always associated with a reduction in functional abilities

correct_answer.text: Thought disorder is probably more evident

correct_answers.text: Thought disorder is probably more evident

questions.explanation: Explanation:Schizophrenia is approximately 3 times more common in those with intellectual disability than in the general population. Age of onset tends to be earlier (mean 23 years). It is more commonly associated with epilepsy, negative symptoms, and impairment of episodic memory. In severe ID there may be unexplained aggression, bizarre behaviour, labile mood, or increased mannerisms and stereotypies. Thought disorder and complex persecutory delusions are probably less evident.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 826.

questions.question_text: Which of the following childhood disorders is more common in girls than in boys?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Rett syndrome is believed to be caused by a dominant X-linked gene. It is a degenerative disorder that almost exclusively affects females.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 103.Persico AM et al. The psychopharmacology of autism spectrum disorder and Rett syndrome. In Handbook of clinical neurology 2019 Jan 1 (Vol. 165, pp. 391-414). Elsevier.

questions.question_text: A couple has a child with Down syndrome. Their risk of having another child with the same syndrome is highest if their first child has which of the following?
questions.explanation: Explanation:In translocation, a fusion occurs of two chromosomes, resulting in a total of 46 chromosomes despite the presence of an extra chromosome 21. The disorder, unlike trisomy 21, is usually inherited and the translocated chromosome may be present in unaffected parents and siblings. The asymptomatic carriers have only 45 chromosomes. When translocation is present, the risk of having a child with Down syndrome is about 1 in 3.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 101.

questions.question_text: An autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance occurs in
questions.explanation: Explanation:Phenylketonuria is a preventable cause of severe intellectual disability. It is an autosomal recessive syndrome characterised by deficits in phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme activity which leads to a buildup of phenylalanine in the body.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 812.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old patient with intellectual disability is to be prescribed lithium for the treatment of his bipolar disorder. Which of the following baseline investigation must be done before initiating therapy?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Given the increased prevalence of seizures in patients with intellectual disability (ID), an EEG is advised. Lithium use for people with epilepsy and ID is cautioned because of its potential to increase the frequency of convulsions at therapeutic doses, and because lithium has marked epileptogenic activity in overdose.Ref: Royal College of Psychiatrists. Prescribing anti-epileptic drugs for people with epilepsy and intellectual disability. 2017.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with atrioventricular septal defects in children?
questions.explanation: Explanation:Congenital heart defects (CHDs) occur in approximately 50% of individuals with Down syndrome (DS), most commonly atrioventricular septal defect (42% of CHDs in individuals with DS), ventricular septal defect (22%) and atrial septal defect (16%).Ref: Antonarakis SE et al. Down syndrome. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2020 Jan;6(1):9.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common feature of Prader-Willi syndrome?

options.text: Near normal IQ in 50% of children

questions.explanation: Explanation:The cardinal features of Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) include severe infantile hypotonia, hyperphagia with the onset of obesity during early childhood if not controlled, developmental delay with learning and behavioural problems, short stature with small hands/feet and hypogonadism/hypogenitalism due to growth hormone and other endocrine deficiencies. Mild craniofacial dysmorphism with enamel hypoplasia and a dry mouth are common. Psychiatric phenotypes, behavioural and autism features correlate with specific PWS genetic subtypes (e.g., autism in those with maternal disomy 15). Cognitive and behavioural problems (tantrums, compulsions, compulsive skin picking) are common. Global developmental delay and mental deficiency (average IQ = 65) occur in nearly all children with PWS.Ref: Butler MG et al. Prader-Willi syndrome-clinical genetics, diagnosis and treatment approaches: an update. Current pediatric reviews. 2019 Nov 1;15(4):207-44.
